def transform(grid):
    g = np.asarray(grid)
    bg = 0 if (g == 0).any() else background(g)
    objs = [o for o in objects(g, bg=bg) if o["colour"] != bg]
    # pick the object with the fewest cells
    small = min(objs, key=lambda o: o["size"])
    y0, x0, y1, x1 = small["box"]

    # stage 1: keep only the smallest block on the original canvas
    stage = np.full_like(g, bg)
    for (y, x) in small["cells"]:
        stage[y, x] = small["colour"]
    emit(stage, "Keep only the smallest block (colour %d); erase all larger blocks" % small["colour"])

    # stage 2: crop to its bounding box, a solid rectangle of its colour
    out = np.full((y1 - y0 + 1, x1 - x0 + 1), small["colour"], dtype=g.dtype)
    emit(out, "Output is the smallest block cropped to its bounding box")
    return out

selection.text: So the rule is: find the object with the fewest cells (the smallest rectangle) and output it, cropped to its bounding box.
The smallest block is never covered by another one (it always lies on top), so its bounding box is exactly a solid rectangle of its colour — which is why the outputs contain no other colour.
The smallest is the 6 block at rows 9–11, columns 7–9 (it overlaps the big 4 block but is on top), so the answer is a 3×3 grid of colour 6.
